The Large Hadron Collider's High-Luminosity era poses a significant problem in managing massive data sets generated at enhanced rates, outstripping analysis capacity and necessitating a shift from local to cloud-based processing for certain tasks. To meet this challenge, a new approach utilizing container technology has been developed to provide user-friendly, secure access to various resources, including storage and compute capabilities. This innovative solution, known as the LHC Computing Centre's LHCv1 service, utilizes containerization to offer a unified interface for local and remote execution, seamless resource integration, and efficient job management, thereby facilitating a substantial increase in processing capacity to meet experimental demands. This comprehensive service not only provides direct access to local resources but also extends its capabilities to external users, enabling the submission of jobs to cloud platforms like CERN's Platform as a Service for experimental collaborations. This hybrid architecture empowers external users to scale their analysis workloads beyond local limits, ensuring prompt integration with local data services and analysis results. This hybrid approach has been successfully implemented and optimized to meet the needs of the High-Luminosity LHC's data-intensive computing demands. To illustrate its effectiveness, a real-world example of its application in processing top quark analysis jobs is presented, demonstrating its scalability and performance in handling diverse workloads across different sites. This containerized infrastructure has the potential to serve as a foundational model for future data management challenges in the High-Luminosity LHC era, enabling seamless scaling up to hundreds of users and facilitating secure, secure, and efficient data-driven workflows. This approach has the added benefit of being adaptable and applicable to various High-Luminosity LHC sites, and its future development plans and prospects for the computing infrastructure of the High-Luminosity LHC are also discussed.

The study of specific superposition methods for linear nonhomogeneous ordinary differential equations reveals that the internal class methods can generate solutions using vectors of associated systems' solutions. A new approach based on the Krylov-Boltyanskii algorithm is introduced to generalize these methods and provide a characterization of their applicability. It is shown that the new method can be viewed as a generalized internal class method, encompassing established approaches such as the power expansion method and the matrix exponentiation method. A numerical example is provided to illustrate the effectiveness of the new approach. Furthermore, the internal class methods can be extended to solve high-order linear constant coefficient differential equations, and a new method based on the Krylov-Boltyanskii algorithm is developed to handle this extension. This new method can generate high-order solutions by combining low-order solutions and is applicable to high-order linear constant coefficient differential equations, regardless of their order or degeneracy. A numerical example is given to demonstrate its practical utility. In addition, the text revisits the internal class methods for first-order linear constant coefficient differential equations, highlighting their broader applicability and potential for generating solutions based on the observation that higher-order linear constant coefficient differential equations can be reduced to sequences of first-order equations. Finally, the text explores the numerical solution of linear linear Volterra differential equations, utilizing the internal class methods to obtain solutions for these equations, given that the corresponding Volterra differential equations' right-hand sides are linear combinations of Volterra kernels, enabling the application of established methods to solve the equations. A numerical example is provided to illustrate the effectiveness of the approach. All the presented methods are implemented in a Julia program. In models of spontaneous symmetry breaking, a unique phenomenon occurs where the scattering amplitudes of low-mass bosons defy conventional expectations when the mass approaches zero, even in the presence of strong interactions. Contrary to the predictions of tree-level effective field theories, this study reveals that the amplitude can be affected by interactions involving four-point vertices, leading to logarithmic corrections to large logarithms originally attributed to collinear divergences. To address this discovery, the authors introduce a novel technique for handling these corrections in the context of soft limit regularization. They demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to a set of soft amplitude identities and show that it successfully maintains their validity, even in the presence of these logarithmic corrections. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of considering these corrections in the context of soft field redefinition and the renormalization of the theory. To facilitate this understanding, the authors provide a detailed explanation of their derivation of the soft photon theorem in the presence of these logarithmic corrections. This study's results have significant implications for the study of effective field theories and the behavior of soft particles within them. They also have important applications in the context of the Large Hadron Collider, particularly in relation to the search for new physics beyond the standard model. However, conventional methods like importance-weighted least-squares estimation are highly sensitive to outliers, limiting their applicability. To overcome this, we explore marginal importance weights as a suitable estimation tool in this setting, yielding regression-based estimators that are more robust to outliers. We demonstrate that these estimators can be used to obtain consistent and asymptotically normal estimates under relatively mild conditions, including situations where the behavior and evaluation sets need not be identical. Furthermore, we show that these estimators can be combined to achieve consistent estimates without needing to specify the behavior distribution, which can be particularly useful in scenarios with unknown behavior distributions. Our research also highlights the challenges of estimating marginal importance weights and suggests a practical approach to doing so. The UNet model, a variant of the traditional U-net architecture, has demonstrated its effectiveness in medical image segmentation tasks. Building upon the original design, researchers have introduced numerous variants in an effort to enhance segmentation performance. While these improvements have primarily focused on modifying the encoder, less attention has been given to the decoder due to the assumption that its performance is inherently stable. However, our study challenges this notion by proposing a new approach to the decoder's component design. Specifically, we introduce the concept of skip connections in the decoder to facilitate communication between features from adjacent blocks, which we found to be critical for accurate segmentation. Our experiments, which involved testing our modified UNet architecture on three datasets, revealed that incorporating these skip connections in the decoder leads to improved performance. Notably, our results show significant gains in evaluation metrics, such as the Dice coefficient and Hausdorff distance, across all three datasets compared to the original UNet. Furthermore, our analysis of the original UNet code revealed that these improvements can be achieved without increasing the complexity of the model. Our findings are expected to be of interest to researchers working in the field of medical image segmentation. Our study demonstrates the independent control over the spin states of a hole spin in a GaAs quantum point wire using a method that utilizes electric field modulation of the hole spin. By varying the gate voltage in the wire, we adjust the potential energy levels and hence the Zeeman sensitivity of the hole spin states, enabling electric field-induced tuning of the Landé g-tensor. Training neural networks on long video sequences is often hindered by the computational expense of running lengthy simulations. To overcome this, we have developed a novel approach called Skip-Sideways, which leverages curvature-based regularization to enable faster-than-real-time training. This approach accelerates training by omitting nearby temporal steps and inserting randomly sampled ones, effectively circumventing the computational limitations of traditional methods. To prevent overfitting, Skip-Sideways incorporates a curvature-based regularization mechanism that penalizes excessive parameter changes, yielding improved generalization capabilities. Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets and network architectures have demonstrated that Skip-Sideways can train neural networks significantly faster than real-time, achieving results comparable to more computationally intensive training strategies. For instance, Skip-Sideways enabled training a ResNet-18 on ImageNet in approximately 1.5 days, whereas the standard approach would take around 10 days. Moreover, Skip-Sideways can be seamlessly integrated into existing frameworks to accelerate training without compromising performance. This paper proposes an error detection system aimed at identifying inaccurate summarizations, allowing for the separation of the accuracy and summarization tasks. By utilizing fine-tuned BERT models to capture semantic meaning in both original documents and summaries, the system detects inaccuracies by measuring semantic discrepancies. The widespread adoption of multimodal databases in artificial intelligence and computer science has led to a significant need for a comprehensive understanding of complex relationships among different modalities, such as text, images, and audio. Unfortunately, existing query languages only focus on basic relationships like similarity and equality, and neglect more subtle connections like causation and substitution. To address this limitation, a new multimodal database model called the Multimodal Object-Relationship-Attribute (MORA) model has been proposed, which incorporates advanced concepts to enable more detailed queries. This model defines novel query languages grounded in first-order logic, including a basic select query language and an advanced aggregate query language, along with a formal foundation for its semantics. To deploy deep learning models on limited resources like smartphones and smart glasses, model pruning is a crucial step that reduces complex models' memory requirements, aligning them with available on-device processing capabilities. Current pruning methods, however, are ineffective because they fail to consider the impact of pruning on a model's architecture and subsequent training performance. This paper introduces a novel, structure-preserving pruning technique that leverages the characteristics of well-pruned and poorly-performing layers to optimize model pruning without compromising performance. Our approach, known as L2P, is a model pruning method that utilizes the second derivatives of loss with respect to model parameters to gauge the importance of layers and their weights, thereby identifying the most effective weights and layers for pruning. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that L2P outperforms leading pruning methods, achieving a significant improvement of up to 5% in accuracy without compromising model compactness. We introduce WikiGUM, a substantial, domain-specific dataset for Entity
Linking, featuring 60,000 sentences drawn from 5 million English Wikipedia articles
covering the universe of entities mentioned across over 1 billion web pages.
Unlike existing datasets, WikiGUM allows entities to possess multiple labels based on
their respective mention frequencies within the Wikipedia labels.
This label diversity is then leveraged to create diverse evaluation metrics
for accurately modeling label uncertainty.
We present WikiGUM as a benchmark for Entity Linking research to address the
persistent challenge of accurately linking web documents to Wikidata's extensive
labelled knowledge base. Our research indicates that current models are far from
achieving optimal performance in this regard.
Our data, code, and evaluation tools are publicly available at
https://github.com/dbpedia/WikiGUM. We anticipate that WikiGUM will serve as a
foundational dataset for Entity Linking research in the future.

Recent advancements in unsupervised reinforcement learning have led to the development of agents capable of adapting to novel tasks without explicit supervision. However, these agents often struggle to achieve optimal performance due to their limited ability to coordinate their actions across different tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce an innovative approach that enables agents to learn a higher-level policy that coordinates low-level skills by leveraging the similarities between tasks. This is achieved by representing skills as a mixture of recurrent neural network policies and incorporating an attention mechanism that modulates the mixing weights. By leveraging the similarities between tasks, the agent can adapt to novel tasks by reconfiguring the mixing weights, thus enabling the development of a higher-level policy that can coordinate low-level skills. The proposed method is applied to the Object Rearrangement task and demonstrates the agent's ability to achieve optimal performance on unseen tasks, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Additionally, the method is shown to facilitate skill generalization, enabling the agent to adapt to novel tasks with minimal training data. The method's effectiveness is further illustrated through ablation studies, demonstrating the agent's ability to adapt to novel tasks with a combination of low-level skills. Overall, the proposed method represents a significant step forward in the development of agents capable of coordinating skills in a flexible and efficient manner. The method's effectiveness is expected to contribute to the development of more adaptable and efficient reinforcement learning agents. The majority of two-dimensional transformations in multi-view detection usually disregard an object's height, projecting all features horizontally without altering their vertical positions.
This simplification leads to significant errors when projecting a reference line in a reference frame onto other frames, causing large discrepancies due to different frame heights.
To address this issue, we introduce a method that accurately accounts for varying frame heights in two steps: first, estimate the height of each object in a reference frame using its vanishing point and dimensions, and then calculate a "frame-independent height" for each object; second, apply a two-dimensional transformation that matches feature heights in both reference and target frames, using a "frame-independent height" for more accurate projections. This method is applied to all reference features, including both detected objects and those from vanishing points, to accurately update reference line projections in other frames, reducing errors caused by frame height differences and enabling more precise detection in various scenarios. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective, with improved results in experiments with both artificial and real-world data. Our code is available for review on GitHub. A video of our results can be viewed here: https://youtu.be/6L6L6L6L6L6. We also provide supplementary material in the appendix. With this method, we achieve a notable improvement of 4.6% mAP over the existing vanishing point-based method, making it a valuable tool in multi-view detection research. Our results are comparable to those of a recent two-dimensional transformation-based method, which achieved a 2.8% improvement. Although both methods show promise, we note that they still fall short of the 3D transformation-based method in terms of performance. Our approach is designed to be complementary to other methods, and we believe it has the potential to be integrated into existing 2D transformation-based methods to achieve even better results. Recent advances in self-supervised learning have led to significant improvements in representation quality, but evaluating these advancements is challenging due to a lack of clear metrics. We propose a new metric to assess the smoothness of the representation manifold in SSL methods, which involves comparing the differences in representation points to those of supervised classifiers. Our results show that self-supervised and fully supervised approaches produce distinct manifolds, with a notable increase in smoothness as the number of labeled data points increases, suggesting that supervised methods can learn more coherent representations. We further investigate the effectiveness of our proposed metric by testing it on various downstream classification tasks and discover that it accurately predicts model performance, aligns with human intuition, and provides a more reliable estimate than existing metrics like linear evaluation. Overall, our work provides a new framework for assessing the smoothness of the representation manifold in SSL methods, enabling more informed decision-making and algorithm development. of modeling complex multi-layered network structures. By leveraging a unique 
message passing mechanism, M-GCN is able to capture the intricate interactions 
between interconnected networks. Furthermore, we propose a novel graph 
representation learning framework that utilizes a dynamic message passing layer

demonstrated to achieve superior performance in various graph-based learning tasks.

across a range of graph-based learning tasks. Finally, we provide in-depth 
insights into the proposed approach through ablation studies and case studies,

improving the performance of graph-based learning tasks. The code for our method

representation learning, which we believe will pave the way for the development

Domain generalization in machine learning is the process of adapting to unseen domains after successful adaptation to known domains. Recent studies have demonstrated that large-scale pre-trained models, specifically foundation models, possess the ability to generalize across domains. Nevertheless, the extent to which these models can generalize is constrained by their performance in the initial domain. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the advantages of foundation models in domain generalization. By utilizing the contrastive learning capabilities of foundation models in conjunction with a novel objective function, we enhance the ability of these models to generalize across domains. Furthermore, we introduce a method for integrating domain knowledge into the pre-trained models, thereby enhancing their performance in the target domain. Experimental results on multiple datasets confirm the effectiveness of our proposed approach, surpassing the performance of existing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, the source code for this method will be made publicly available after its acceptance. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of our method to better understand its performance. Our approach can be applied to various domain generalization tasks, including but not limited to, the visual domain adaptation problem. A novel approach to objective image dehazing evaluation is proposed, which
involves extracting three types of image features: spatial, frequency, and time
domain features. By combining these features, the method assesses the quality of
dehazed images. First, the image is converted into the YUV domain and separated
into the luminance and chrominance channel. Then, the luminance channel is
transformed into the time and frequency domain. Subsequently, the proposed method
selects the best-performing channel and features from each domain to predict the
haze intensity. Through the use of a linear regression model based on least square
optimization, the method estimates the actual amount of haze in the image. Our
results demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses existing image dehazing
evaluation metrics. Additionally, the source code is available for download on GitHub.

This research also identifies areas where improvement is needed for future neural network models, particularly in refining the word embedding process and reducing model complexity. Finally, the study provides insights on the interpretability of neural network predictions, revealing that the models tend to learn and focus on irrelevant features, which can hinder their ability to accurately forecast stock movements. Ultimately, the findings suggest that neural network models require continued development to achieve optimal results. This research proposes an innovative control method that enables a quadruped robot to adapt to three-dimensional uneven terrains by leveraging internal sensing of the robot's posture and the position of its feet. A unified control system is developed, integrating balance maintenance, movement control, and foot placement strategies to facilitate the robot's ability to navigate uneven terrain while maintaining stability and mobility. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through successful navigation on three-dimensional uneven terrains with complex obstacles, such as rocks and stairs, achieved by a RAVEN robot. This research showcases the robot's ability to adapt to and navigate on complex three-dimensional uneven terrains with obstacle avoidance capabilities. Our approach involves identifying distinct features in the majority class and incorporating them into the learning process to ensure a more balanced representation.
Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in multiple real-world datasets. We investigate generating robust image classification models that can withstand certain types of input modifications. Unlike typical attacks like randomly perturbing pixels, our goal is to create adversarial examples by manipulating image content in a meaningful way, such as altering objects or their positions within an image. To achieve this, we focus on a type of attack involving grahmic transformations that alter the image content without introducing noise or clutter. We demonstrate that existing defenses against this type of attack are not effective and that our proposed defense, based on an ensemble of trained models, significantly outperforms individual models on a key benchmark, achieving a 62.3% accuracy under strong attack conditions. Notably, our ensemble outperforms individual models by a substantial margin, with an improvement of 10% over the best individual model. Additionally, we examine the effectiveness of our ensemble defense against various types of attacks and find that it provides strong protection against grahmic attacks but is more vulnerable to other types of attacks. We also show that our ensemble defense is effective against a range of image classification tasks and can be applied to a variety of models, including those trained on different types of data, such as MNIST and CIFAR-10. Event cameras have proven to be highly effective in detecting fast-moving objects like drone propellers due to their high sensitivity to intense brightness. However, current event cameras lack the capability to produce detailed depth information, making them less practical for everyday use. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel fusion framework that combines data from both classical RGB-D cameras and event cameras to generate precise depth information for objects. Our framework utilizes a pixel-level fusion technique, where RGB data is used to identify matching pixels and depth information is retrieved from RGB images, resulting in clear and detailed 3D reconstructions of drone propellers. We also propose a robust object detection method to ensure accurate identification of these fast-moving objects. Notably, our method outperforms existing event-based detection methods, not only in depth information, but also in object detection speed and accuracy. Moreover, we have successfully demonstrated real-time object detection, where our system can detect propellers at a rate of 30 frames per second. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted to validate the performance of our method and achieve state-of-the-art results. The techniques developed here can be easily adapted to analyze the Dark Matter candidates in a comprehensive manner, providing a more in-depth exploration of the various models and their distinctive features. Our objective is to develop a method that integrates multiple predictors, 
yielding superior performance on a particular learning task. Current techniques, 
however, rely on either heuristic or model-based approaches, which are limited by their 
ignorance of the relationships between predictors or their inability to account for 
the complexities of the prediction models. To address this, we've created a new 
algorithm that constructs an information-theoretic objective to combine predictors, 
thereby maximizing the overall predictive power of the prediction ensemble. 

Our algorithm, called Generalized Maximum Mutual Information (GM-MI), 
determines the optimal combination of predictors that results in the highest 
information gain about the target labels. To achieve this, we've developed a 
flexible framework that can work with a wide range of predictors, including neural 
networks, logistic regression, and random forests, as well as their combinations. 
We've also tested GM-MI on various real-world datasets and found that it performs 
better than other top-performing ensemble methods, both in terms of accuracy and 
model complexity. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that GM-MI can be applied to the 
problem of selecting the right predictors, rather than combining them, which is a 
crucial step in building effective prediction models. Through our analysis, 
we've shown that GM-MI can be used to assess the quality of the predictors, 
identify the ones that contribute the most to the ensemble, and even optimize the 
ensemble by selecting the right set of predictors, all of which can be done using 
GM-MI. Our results highlight the potential benefits of GM-MI in building more robust 
prediction models that can handle complex relationships between predictors, 
achieve better generalization, and provide a deeper understanding of the 
prediction models. We believe that GM-MI will become a valuable tool for the 
research community to develop more effective and efficient prediction models,

Additionally, our implementation of Wink in an encrypted chat application demonstrates its real-world applicability. Furthermore, Wink's source code is available for review and examination at a provided website. This research also examines potential limitations and future enhancements to the Wink system. A graph's $r$-hued chromatic number is the minimum number of colors needed to fully color its vertices, with each color set of at most $r$ distinct hues. This generalizes previous $r$-hued chromatic number results and, in the case of $r=1$, reduces to a well-known bound on graph chromatic numbers. We further show this upper bound is tight for large $r$ values on a specific graph type and provide upper and lower bounds for $r=2,3$ in different graph types, with additional bounds for large $r$ values. Lastly, we discuss computational complexity of finding the $r$-hued chromatic number and provide bounds on its complexity. This research is the first to explore $r$-hued graph coloring and demonstrates potential for color-efficient algorithms when the $r$-hued chromatic number is known. We also propose a method to color graphs efficiently with a fixed number of hues. However, their performance in generating a predictive kernel for classification tasks in high-dimensional spaces is not well-documented. In this study, we investigate the properties of kernels derived from these ensembles in relation to classification accuracy and training time across various data types and parameter settings. Our results indicate that while they produce competitive outcomes in certain scenarios, their performance in high-dimensional continuous data settings is often inferior to support vector machines. Moreover, the effectiveness of these ensembles in these environments is highly sensitive to various factors including feature selection, feature interaction depth, and ensemble size, which can lead to suboptimal results. Interestingly, the kernels produced by these ensembles can be combined with those of support vector machines to achieve better predictive performance. Ultimately, the effectiveness of these ensembles in these environments is heavily dependent on the specific design of their architectures and the careful selection of their parameters to mitigate these risks. Our research provides a valuable foundation for further investigation into the potential applications of these ensembles in kernel-based spaces. In remote sensing imaging systems, pan-sharpening plays a critical role in enhancing the spatial and spectral details of panchromatic images. A novel deep convolutional neural network, known as the pan-sharpening network (PSN), has been developed to address this challenge. The PSN model is composed of a multi-scale network (MSN) and a local detail network (LDN). The MSN extracts high-level semantic information from MSI images, while the LDN recovers detailed information from pan images. A multi-scale convolutional layer is introduced to improve the MSN's ability to capture semantic information, by utilizing the MSN's multiple scales simultaneously. The MSN and LDN are then combined to produce a pan-chromatic image. A novel loss function, incorporating both L1 and L2 norms, is also proposed to evaluate the pan-chromatic image. Experiment results demonstrate the PSN's superior performance compared to other leading methods. The PSN model and experiment codes are available online. Expert combination in modern neural networks is often achieved through mixture of experts (MoE) networks, which consist of a gate and a mixture layer. These gates determine which experts to use for specific input elements, but they can be overly confident and less effective when the gate's output is highly concentrated. To address this limitation, we introduce gating dropout (GDrop), a modified MoE approach that incorporates random dropouts during training to encourage more diverse and robust gate outputs. This is done by dropping input elements with a specified probability. As a result, the gate's output becomes more uncertain, and the model learns to utilize its full range of experts, leading to enhanced accuracy and robustness. Our experiments demonstrate GDrop's superiority in text classification tasks, particularly with large expert pools, and the code is publicly available on GitHub. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a leading approach for processing graph-structured data. Despite their success, they often struggle with the high computational requirements of their message passing layers, particularly when dealing with complex graph representations. This limitation has a significant impact on the scalability of GNNs to larger graphs. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel framework that utilizes a hierarchical graph representation and combines node embeddings through message passing. Our approach, called HiGH, is a versatile and efficient GNN architecture that can be applied to various tasks. HiGH achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on standard benchmarks while significantly reducing the computational requirements, thus enabling it to process larger graphs efficiently. Experimental results on different graph classification tasks demonstrate that HiGH can learn effective representations in a more efficient manner than existing methods. Our analysis highlights the benefits of HiGH in terms of its ability to handle large-scale graphs and its improved generalizability. HiGH is made available as an open-source package, allowing for easy integration with other GNNs. We anticipate that our framework will facilitate the development of more scalable and generalizable GNNs for real-world applications. This paper introduces a method to convert high-level language specifications into safe and efficient control systems for autonomous vehicles operating in environments with obstacles. The approach relies on linear-time temporal logic for finite traces, incorporates a planning technique called probabilistic motion planning, and provides a way to generate safe and reliable control systems from formal requirements. By applying this method, we demonstrate its ability to effectively translate system properties, regardless of their complexity or number, into practical control systems for mobile robots. The performance of our approach is further validated through experiments using real-world and synthetic specifications. The provided code allows users to easily integrate the developed solution into mobile platforms and assess their effectiveness in real-world and simulated environments. The necessary code can be accessed at https://github.com/irichir/autonomous_navigation.git. The associated project can be reached at https://sites.google.com/view/autonomous_navigation2022. In the context of tensor regression, we explore the challenge of estimating a linear relationship between a symmetric, positive-definite tensor and a random response variable. We introduce a novel statistical method called importance sketching, where the key idea is to create a sampling distribution that closely resembles the input tensor. By applying importance sketching to specific types of tensors, we derive optimal sketching complexity, provide strategies for constructing these distributions, and establish non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds for recovery accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that importance sketching can be a more efficient data sampling technique compared to traditional random projections, especially in the setting of tensor regression. Additionally, we discuss the feasibility of extending this approach to handle higher-order tensors and discuss potential research avenues for future investigation. As an example, we apply importance sketching to the task of image classification using TensorCNN and show that it yields better or comparable results to those obtained by conventional random projections. Autonomous vehicles rely heavily on accurate local localization techniques to navigate unfamiliar roads safely. However, traditional methods using 2D images are often limited by the lack of depth information. To overcome this challenge, a new deep learning network is proposed for 3D LiDAR-based place recognition, specifically designed to efficiently process large point clouds while minimizing energy consumption. By employing a multi-channel feature extraction approach, the network is trained to extract essential geometric features from multi-channel point clouds. To enhance the network's robustness to variations in lighting conditions, a novel feature fusion strategy is developed, enabling the recognition of 3D LiDAR scans in different environments. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the proposed system's superior performance, including high accuracy and robustness to lighting variations, as well as its ability to function effectively on limited resource hardware. Furthermore, a real-world autonomous driving experiment is conducted to validate the proposed system's performance in practical scenarios. The results show that the proposed system outperforms existing methods in terms of localization accuracy and computational efficiency. The code and data used in this research are made available online for further study. A video showcasing the proposed system's performance in real-world driving conditions can be found on YouTube. The project's webpage includes additional information, including a video, results, and a running demo. For more details, please visit https://sites.google.com/view/lidar-place-recognition. As teams face increased competition in rapidly changing environments, there is a pressing need to understand the impact of cognitive stress on team performance. Our study investigates the relationship between cognitive stress and team performance in a dynamic context by analyzing the interaction between two individuals working together to complete a task. Our findings show that as cognitive stress levels rise, team performance improves, but our results also indicate a negative correlation between stress levels and various aspects of team interaction, including the frequency of social interactions, the amount of information shared, and the speed of team response in a dynamic game-based task. Our research has significant implications for enhancing collaborative robotics applications, particularly in high-stakes environments where teams must work under increased pressure. Our study suggests that effectively managing cognitive stress within a team can have a direct impact on team performance, making it an essential factor to consider in the design of collaborative robotics systems. The findings of our study can serve as a foundation for future research in the field of human-robot collaboration. This research offers a straightforward calibration technique for ensuring a trial design maintains its intended Type I Error rate at alpha.  The method involves calculating an adjustment factor for the entire design based on the critical values of its individual components.  The proposed method is illustrated through an example using a two-sample Z-test and is available in the form of R code.  An accompanying appendix provides the formula for calculating design alpha in the special case of normal distributions with known and equal variances.  Our approach is compared to the work of Fdr0 in the flexswitch R package developed by Gupta and Jun.  The method is further extended to handle non-central test scenarios, including two-sample non-parametric and one-sample t-tests with unknown variances.  The method is available through an R package called designcalibration, version 1.0, on the CRAN repository, with additional documentation on GitHub at https://github/designcalibration.  The method is validated through simulation studies for non-central z-tests.  The method is applied to a real-world example involving the analysis of a biomarker for cancer treatment response using a two-sample t-test.  The method is available for download from the CRAN repository, version 1.2, for use in R.  The accompanying R code is provided in the supplementary appendix. The use of mathematical models to describe the mechanics of soft tissue is widespread, but choosing the most suitable model is a challenging task. In this research, a variety of models were tested to see how well they predicted the stretching patterns in pig aortic valves under different conditions. Historically, the models used to describe such tissues have included the Neo-Hookean, Gent, Vogel, and Yeoh models. By using a Bayesian approach, it was found that the Yeoh model is the most accurate for describing pig aortic valves, especially in a specific part of the tissue. This model's accuracy is consistent across a range of testing methods and is not affected by the age or size of the tissue samples examined. While the Yeoh model is the most accurate, it's also found that it can be simplified into a model with three variables to achieve similar results. This paper presents a novel distributed learning-based control method for multi-agent systems governed by linear dynamics with a leader. The proposed algorithm is effective in achieving a formation task where agents maintain a specific relative position through a learned control action. Our algorithm uniquely allows each agent to independently determine its reference position and compute the control signal solely based on its local measurements and a predetermined linear transformation, without requiring global system knowledge or complex computations. Our approach is demonstrated to produce a stable formation solution, and its efficacy is evaluated through a connection test underlain by the theory of linear matrix inequalities. Moreover, our method offers a substantial computational cost reduction, up to a linear complexity, compared to existing control methods for multi-agent systems. The proposed algorithm is further validated through simulations involving both connected and unconnected multi-agent formations. Ultimately, our method is shown to provide a more efficient and scalable solution for multi-agent formation control compared to existing methods. We introduce a new first-order constraint solver capable of handling complex multi-rigid body systems with diverse geometric constraints. By formulating constraints in a structured format, we leverage the properties of semi-algebraic sets to develop a solver that's based on first-order logical formulas and efficient non-linear optimization techniques. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in tackling challenging problems that elude state-of-the-art solvers. We introduce a new approach to automatically selecting relevant data sources, including a combination of any type and number of potential data sources, which can potentially increase the detection speed and accuracy of an existing syndromic surveillance system. This method involves using a neural network model that can identify the most useful data sources for detecting a specific disease, then using that information to improve disease monitoring. We demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting influenza in France by selecting the best data sources for detecting the disease across the country using daily reports from 12 sources. We have evaluated the pressure in the quantum chromodynamics phase with two flavors of dynamical quarks to a precision of $g^6$. Building upon a perturbative expression for the pressure to a precision of $g^4$, first established by Gertie Schmelling, we have determined the remaining leading logarithmic contributions up to a precision of $g^6$. These contributions arise from the Mellin-Barnes integral, originally used by Gertie Schmelling, which expresses the pressure in terms of gamma functions. To compute the remaining leading logarithmic contributions, we have derived an asymptotic expansion for the associated gamma function, and subsequently applied it to derive the pressure to a precision of $g^6$. Our result is consistent with recent lattice QCD calculations performed by the Borsanyi group. Furthermore, our findings also validate the perturbative perturbation theory results, originally predicted by Yagi and Ito, provided the coupling constant remains below a critical value of $\alpha_s \approx 0.290$. Ultimately, our work establishes a crucial foundation for extending the perturbative pressure to a precision of $g^8$. The underlying mathematical framework developed in this study is also anticipated to be valuable in facilitating future research. We examine multiple polylogarithms in relation to holomorphic one-forms on their universal abelian covering and establish a method for computing one-forms on arbitrary trees. By applying this approach, we derive a one-form representation for the Goncharov unit collection and show that multiple polylogarithms exhibit affine connections with respect to their arguments, which we further simplify in terms of the pre-images of a specific map defined by the polylogarithm in question. Furthermore, the connection between multiple polylogarithms and one-forms is extended to include non-positive arguments through a non-linear covering map, which enables the computation of one-forms for the Euler polylogarithm and results in a new formula for its real line extension. Additionally, we establish a new formula for computing one-forms of the Euler 2-polylogarithm. Our research also explores the geometric interpretation of the Stokes matrices through an analysis of the affine connection framework. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our findings on the quantum A and B functions. This work is complemented by a companion paper that provides a direct computation of one-forms for the polylogarithms considered in this study. Moreover, the accompanying document provides a collection of exercises that outline the equivalence between different geometric representations of multiple polylogarithms proposed within this research. Our research is also available in a more detailed form in a companion book titled "Multiple Polylogarithms, Part I". The problem of identifying quantum states can be reinterpreted as a perfect matching problem under specific vertex color constraints. This perspective allows us to derive two new algorithms, one based on fast algorithms for perfect matching and the other utilizing a linear programming approach. Additionally, we explore the potential of using semi-definite programming to improve existing algorithms, resulting in a theoretical speedup for matching-based quantum-state identification methods. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of the interplay between quantum-state identification and perfect matching, leading to new insights into the computational complexity of the matching graph. Moreover, we demonstrate that quantum-state identification can be approximated with high efficiency for a wide range of scenarios, and highlight further avenues for investigation. This paper is a comprehensive extension of the authors' earlier work, incorporating new ideas and results presented at the MPSOC 2020 conference. Subsequent revisions have led to a significant improvement in the approximation factor for the semi-definite programming approach. Notably, we have also developed a new algorithm for matching-based quantum-state identification, which offers a near-optimal solution for a broad spectrum of cases. Deep learning models excel in extracting features from data, converting it into
representations suitable for classification, but often fall short in real-world scenarios
due to limitations such as limited data, adversarial attacks, and adversarial environments.
This issue can be addressed by leveraging principles from animal intelligence research,
specifically, 'Occam's bias', where models learn to make educated guesses from limited
information. Inspired by the neural patterns of rodents, our proposed method uses
a neural network architecture equipped with a novel loss function and an adaptive
weight decay mechanism to enhance generalization in deep learning models.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly boosts the
generalization capabilities of state-of-the-art deep learning models on a range of
image classification tasks. Notably, it also enhances their resistance to adversarial
attacks and performance in low-shot learning scenarios. The accompanying code is
available at https://github.com/UK-Castle-ML/OccamsBias. A more detailed explanation
of the methodology and results can be found in the supplementary materials. A video
demonstrating key findings can be viewed at https://youtu.be/8Jj4GKu2k7Q. A blog
post providing an in-depth overview is available at https://ukcastleml.github.io/2022/occamsbias.

We establish Hessian and Laplacian comparison theorems for compact metric spaces with a measure that is invariant under isometry groups. These theorems naturally encompass comparisons for both for Riemannian manifolds and graphs, with theorems for graphs being proved by reducing them to directed graph analogues using the Gromov-Hausdorff distance. Additionally, we derive a comparison theorem for heat semigroups on graphs by first proving it for heat semigroups on invariant measure spaces via the discrete heat equation. These comparisons ultimately enable us to generalize a previously established Hessian comparison theorem from Riemannian manifolds to compact metric spaces with the aforementioned invariance property. These comparisons have implications for the Laplacian and heat semigroup spectra of graphs, allowing us to generalize a previously established lower bound for eigenvalues of Riemannian manifolds to compact metric spaces with the invariance property. Ultimately, we use these findings to derive a lower bound for eigenvalues of the discrete Laplacian in the universal cover of compact metric spaces with the invariance property. The concept of leaky-forcing in graph theory was first introduced by Haggkvist and Malmborg, and later expanded upon by a group of researchers. A $(d-2)$-leaky forcing configuration within a graph is a subset with a specific property such that any two edges form a forcing pair, and any additional edge connected to this subset affects at least d-1 of these pairs. The maximum size of the smallest leaky forcing configuration necessary for covering the entire graph is known as its leaky forcing number. The authors of this study have demonstrated that for the $d$-dimensional hypercube, the leaky forcing number can be at most $d+1$. In software development, features are often temporarily enabled to test, refine, or remove them. However, these features can interfere with one another when integrated, causing errors in the code. To address this issue, developers use feature toggles, temporary mechanisms that enable or disable features. Despite their common use, little is known about how frequently features are combined with these toggles active. Understanding this behavior can help teams manage feature-related issues more effectively. To investigate this knowledge gap, we conducted a large-scale study of 1,011 feature toggles across 30 open-source projects. Our analysis reveals that most features are combined with their associated toggles. Additionally, we found that these toggles are often used to test, develop, and measure features. While most features are compatible with their associated toggers, we identified 7% of the features we examined as causing conflicts when used in conjunction with one another. To gain further insight into this issue, we also conducted a survey of 74 developers, which further highlights the need for better understanding of feature interactions. By studying this behavior, we can help teams manage feature-related issues more effectively, leading to more reliable software. To facilitate this process, we have developed a tool called FeatureToggles, which provides detailed information about feature interactions. Our research findings suggest that developers should consider considering the potential interactions between features when designing their features and these temporary mechanisms. Moreover, we believe that this research can be used to develop more effective tools and practices for managing feature-related issues in software development. Currently, diagnosis methods are invasive and often lead to overdiagnosis due to their inaccuracy. To address these challenges, our research focuses on developing non-invasive machine learning models for Alzheimer's detection using speech recordings from the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center's database. By applying various feature extraction methods and model architectures, we found that our best-performing model achieved impressive results, demonstrating an accuracy of 96% in distinguishing between healthy individuals and those with Alzheimer's at the onset. Furthermore, our findings suggest that users' susceptibility to emotional contagion is influenced by their exposure to such influencers, as evidenced by the increased adoption of positive emotions when users interact with many others. This work also highlights the potential for social media platforms to mitigate the spread of social emotions by implementing measures such as limiting users' exposure to highly influential figures or promoting critical thinking in online interactions. Our research provides a foundational understanding of how social media can facilitate emotional contagion, offering a framework for designing effective interventions to mitigate its impact. This study is the first to empirically examine the role of social media influencers in spreading emotions to their followers, demonstrating the importance of considering influence in online interactions. Our research also underscores the need for a more nuanced understanding of how social media platforms can be leveraged to promote positive behaviors and reduce negative ones. Finally, our findings highlight the importance of future research into the computational study of social emotions and their role in shaping human behavior. This work has the potential to provide a deeper understanding of human behavior and its impact on society, enabling the development of more effective interventions to promote positive behaviors and reduce negative ones. This study addresses the issue of maintaining confidentiality in adversarial educational settings through the development of a privacy-aware learning framework. A model incorporating both local differential privacy and information-theoretic privacy is introduced to examine the balance between privacy and utility. Two types of constraints are considered: one based on the Cramer-Rao lower bound and the other on the mean squared error of the estimator. The effects of data distribution types and sampling methods on privacy-utility trade-offs are thoroughly investigated. Additionally, the study compares the utilization of simulated and real-world data in this context. A comprehensive analysis of the trade-off between privacy and utility is presented, including local differential privacy and information-theoretic privacy. Simulation results demonstrate the potential of this framework to mitigate privacy risks while meeting practical requirements. The findings of this research are expected to provide valuable insights for practitioners in the field of adversarial learning. This work is part of a broader research project that examines the interplay between privacy and utility in educational data analysis. Future investigations will build upon this framework to explore its practical applications in adversarial learning. The development of language learning materials in English is well-documented, yet resources for lesser-known languages often lack and languages with limited financial support face significant challenges in creating such content due to scarcity of funds and qualified specialists. In order to address this, our team has compiled a comprehensive set of language learning materials for Tatar, a language predominantly spoken in Tatarstan, Russia, despite being a language of over one million speakers globally. In this research, we outline the process of creating these resources, specifically a dictionary, grammar book, and language learning course for both children and adults, while highlighting the difficulties we encountered along the way and offering guidance to those who wish to create similar language learning materials for other languages in the future. Additionally, our experience has shown that collaboration with language experts, whether local or international, is key to creating effective language learning materials. As a result, our project has successfully partnered with local Tatar language experts and an online dictionary, grammar, and language learning course are now available online for use by the global Tatar language community. All of our resources are available online at https://tatochka.ru/. This research will be of interest to linguists and enthusiasts of the Tatar language and those who are engaged in the creation of language learning materials for languages spoken by smaller or less represented groups. It is also expected that the methods and techniques used in this project can be applied to other similar language learning initiatives. Keywords: language learning materials, Tatar language, online dictionary, grammar book, course creation, language pedagogy.

Transformers have revolutionized computer vision tasks by leveraging attention-based models, particularly those incorporating self-attention to capture global information and capture long-range dependencies. A significant innovation in computer vision, the Transformer architecture has been successfully applied in tasks such as image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. However, traditional Transformers are memory-hungry and computationally expensive due to quadratic complexity in attention mechanisms, limiting their adoption in resource-constrained environments. In response, we introduce a lightweight, efficient Transformer model for image classification that incorporates a novel, linear-complexity attention approach using spatial attention and channel-wise attention. The proposed model significantly reduces computational complexity while outperforming state-of-the-art classification with minimal parameters. We also develop a high-performance variant of the model, which achieves superior results on ImageNet-1K while reducing the number of FLOPs compared to the original model. Furthermore, we demonstrate the model's robustness in noisy data, making it a promising choice for real-world applications. The relationship between galaxy cluster mass and observable properties serves as a crucial tool for analyzing the large-scale structure of the universe. This research focuses on the impact of mass-observable relation (MoR) uncertainties on constraints of cosmological parameters, particularly when using scaling relations that are not linear. We employed a Markov Chain Monte Carlo approach to model galaxy cluster data, incorporating the halo model, and examined how variations in the MoR impact constraints of parameters, including the matter density and dark energy parameters, in addition to redshift distribution and mass observation bias. Our findings indicate that scaling relations that deviate from a linear relationship can significantly affect the accuracy of constraints, potentially leading to an error of up to 4σ in the estimation of σ8 and σ8\omega_0. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that a non-linear mass-observable relation can also influence the measurement of w0 and w1. This framework has the potential to unlock the full potential of massive networks, enabling the discovery of their inner workings and properties. Current online recommendation lists often only display the top-rated items from their personal models, which raises concerns about fairness towards less appealing items. These less favored items might be shown unnecessarily, especially if they are not well-represented in the personal model. To address this issue, we propose a new method to assess and control the ranking bias in personalization lists. Our approach relies on a measure of the expected value of fairness, which is calculated by comparing the average performance of each item across all possible personal models with the performance of the top-rated items from those models. To make this fair, we incorporate fairness constraints into the optimization problem of building personal models, which can be solved efficiently with a new algorithm that uses gradient-based optimization. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach successfully minimizes bias in personalization lists while maintaining their overall usefulness. To promote further research in this area, we have released a new dataset of online ranking examples. Our code for experimentation is also available on GitHub. We introduce an innovative low-rank structure-based approach for solving the challenge of blind super-resolution. Our method is built on the concept that high-resolution image patches can be accurately represented using a limited set of basis vectors, which can be derived from a low-rank matrix factorization model incorporating total variation regularization. Through numerical analysis, we demonstrate that this model can be efficiently optimized using an accelerated proximal gradient method, resulting in fast and efficient convergence. Our approach is further enhanced by incorporating a non-local means algorithm to reduce artifacts at object boundaries in the final restored image. Experimental results from both simulated and real-world data reveal that our proposed algorithm surpasses existing techniques in terms of image recovery performance. Additionally, the structure-based feature map derived from our low-rank model can be effectively utilized for image super-resolution inpainting, yielding superior restoration results in comparison to other state-of-the-art methods. A thorough comparison with 7 benchmark image inpainting algorithms is also provided. It is worth noting that our proposed image inpainting technique can be extended to solve the problem of high-resolution image recovery from partial Fourier data. This extension is achieved by first transforming the problem into a low-rank matrix recovery problem, and then leveraging the efficiency of our initial approach to obtain superior restoration results in comparison to other state-of-the-art methods. A comprehensive comparison with 5 benchmark image inpainting algorithms is included in the supplementary material.   $\frac{\partial a}{\partial \nu}|_{\partial D}=0$, 
  $\left\lvert \nabla a \rvert\rvert_{\partial D}=1$, 
  where $D$ is a bounded domain with a $C^2$ boundary. 
  We establish that for a threshold value of $a^{*}=\left(\frac{n-2}{n}\right)^{\frac{n}{n+4}}$ 
  (which is the critical exponent of the Sobolev inequality), 
  a solution to the given problem exists for values of $a$ strictly between this threshold and 0. 
  This result is obtained by analyzing the inhomogeneous problem in a more general context using a monotonicity method. 
  We also demonstrate that a solution to the given problem does not exist for values of $a$ below the threshold. 
  Furthermore, we show that the existence or non-existence of a solution to the given problem is determined by the shape of the boundary of the domain $D$. 
  Specifically, we find that the problem admits a solution for values of $a$ below the threshold if and only if $D$ is a convex domain.

  Conversely, we find that the problem does not admit a solution for values of $a$ below the threshold if $D$ is a concave domain.

In federated learning, a central server trains a collective model by gathering gradients from diverse, non-colluding clients. Although this process is designed to preserve client privacy, it can be vulnerable to biases stemming from differing client characteristics. This paper delves into the issue of fairness and security within federated training, showing that various real-world client distributions can lead to backdoor attacks. A new defensive model is proposed to counter these vulnerabilities, which leverages gradient-based techniques in combination with a unique randomization process. This method is demonstrated to effectively neutralize backdoor contaminants and retain most of the trained model's functionality. Performance evaluations are conducted across multiple benchmark datasets, highlighting the proposed defense mechanism's efficacy in various real-world scenarios. Additionally, analysis is provided to explain how the defense counteracts backdoor attacks, and its applicability is demonstrated through extensive experiments. This research aims to advance our understanding of the interplay between fairness and security in federated learning, paving the way for further exploration of this complex topic. Speech recognition systems for low-resource languages often struggle due to limited data availability, making it difficult to create effective models. A possible solution is to leverage data from a related language using transfer learning, but this approach can be limited if there are significant linguistic differences between languages. Our research explores using few-shot learning to address this challenge, enabling speech recognition models to learn from very small datasets. We developed a novel method, Leveraging BERT for Few-shot Speech Recognition (LiBFSR), which utilizes BERT to create models that can accurately recognize speech in low-resource languages using few-shot transfer. Our experiments demonstrate that LiBFSR achieves state-of-the-art results in several low-resource languages with as little as 1% of available data, and even surpasses the performance of a monolingual English model in 1-shot learning. Our findings indicate that LiBFSR offers a promising solution for cross-lingual speech recognition in low-resource settings. The project's code and data are publicly available for further research and application. Our research has significant implications for creating speech recognition systems for low-resource languages, making them more accessible to a broader range of people. Analyzing financial markets, particularly forecasting stock price fluctuations, is a complex task due to the inherent high noise levels in financial time-series data, which makes it difficult to establish meaningful relationships between variables. Despite the limitations, deep learning techniques have shown potential in modeling financial data, despite their sensitivity to sequence length. This study investigates the effectiveness of using GRUs to predict stock price movements, employing a GRU-based approach for both single-stock trading and the simultaneous evaluation of multiple stocks, and compares its performance with other baseline methods. Our results indicate that GRUs yield superior outcomes, particularly for single-stock trading across various parameter settings. Conversely, our multi-granularity model, which incorporates both high and low-resolution data, produces better results than the single-granularity model, highlighting the value of combining multiple levels of financial information. Notably, our approach can be adapted to handle an unlimited number of stocks. Experimental outcomes suggest that GRUs outperform other techniques, achieving an average accuracy of 53.2% in single-granularity experiments and 53.5% in multi-granularity experiments. Overall, our findings demonstrate the potential of GRUs in predicting financial price movements. Federated learning's personalization challenge involves training unique machine learning models for each user. A recent approach, personalized federated learning using hypernetworks (PFLHN), has shown promise by allowing each user's model to be represented as the application of a personal neural network, or hypernetwork, to a general base model. However, this approach's effectiveness depends on the large variation in user data, as it results in better performance compared to conventional methods when this condition is met. Conversely, PFLHN's performance is inferior to other methods when the variation in user data is limited. A proposed solution to address this issue is a new approach, on-the-fly personalization (OTFPFLHN), which allows each user's hypernetwork to be dynamically updated based on their specific data, thereby improving performance when the variation in user data is limited. Experimental results on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate OTFPFLHN's superiority over PFLHN in this scenario and its comparable performance to PFLHN when the variation in user data is high. Additionally, OTFPFLHN's ability to update each user's hypernetwork online in a single global round eliminates the need for repeated rounds, making it more scalable than PFLHN. A key finding in this study is that OTFPFLHN's ability to achieve comparable performance to PFLHN when the variation in user data is high, and its superiority in low-variation scenarios, is attributed to the ability to adapt the hypernetwork to changing user data. Experimental results also show that OTFPFLHN's ability to adapt to changing user data is more effective than PFLHN's one-shot learning approach. Overall, OTFPFLHN offers a more scalable and flexible solution for personalization in federated learning. A recent study found that BERT's translation component is responsible for its cross-lingual transfer ability, but its shared knowledge component is often overlooked despite being essential for tasks like natural language understanding. This paper investigates the cross-lingual transfer ability of BERT's translation component and shared knowledge component separately, and the results show that the shared knowledge component is more crucial for natural language understanding. However, existing methods for pretraining shared knowledge are limited due to their reliance on parallel data, which is often scarce in under-resourced languages. A new method is proposed that leverages monolingual data to pretrain shared knowledge and translation modules, which can be trained end-to-end. This new method is effective across different languages, including those with limited available data, and can be used to improve the accuracy of tasks like sentiment analysis without requiring parallel data. A key component of the method is a novel loss function that encourages the translation module and shared knowledge component to develop distinct representations. Experimental results show that the proposed method can improve the accuracy of natural language understanding tasks, including sentiment analysis, by up to 2.2 points. This study introduces the It\^oWave vocoder model, a more accurate approach
that incorporates the It\^o process, offering a more realistic representation
of wavelet coefficients compared to the Gaussian process-based method.
The model is parameterized by a Wiener process, whose values are estimated
using a neural network trained on log-scale wavelet coefficients and is
unrelated to the original signal's phase. The study assesses the quality of
two It\^oWave models, one with a fixed and another with a trainable signal
variance, demonstrating that they yield high-quality speech reconstruction
results, with the trainable model showing a PESQ score of 3.86. This score is
closer to that of the Wavelet Waveform Audio Codec, with the model also
showing a 9.5\% decrease in computational complexity compared to the
Gaussian process-based model. The It\^oWave model is also found to be more
efficient, with a 2.5\% decrease in the number of neural network parameters and
a 2.5\% decrease in the storage requirements for wavelet coefficients. The
study also highlights the potential of the It\^oWave model in generating
speech samples with a PESQ score of 3.80, surpassing the performance of WaveNet.

We then investigate the relationship between these structures and isometries within symmetric spaces. A primary reason for this difficulty is the lack of connection between language and the complex geometric domain of robotic motion. Experimental results demonstrate the potential of this method in creating versatile robotic systems that can be easily programmed using everyday language through both simulated and real-world tests.  Key outcomes of this research include the development of language-based motion control that can be extended to various robots, the identification of effective language constructs, and the implementation of a real-world system that can be easily installed and operated. We present a gradient iterative solver for symmetric generalized eigenvalue problems under relaxed assumptions on the problem matrices. Convergence is demonstrated under the condition that the inverse Hessian is bounded by a positive definite Hessian. Our approach is grounded in the concept of exterior point optimization in infinite dimensional spaces and leverages geometric properties to devise an efficient algorithm. Both theoretical and practical advantages can be expected, as our method converts an infinite-dimensional problem into a finite-dimensional one, utilizing a suitable metric space. primarily due to the presence of distracting elements, varying lighting conditions,

indoor surveillance environments. This method is founded on the principle

surroundings. Utilizing a cutting-edge semantic segmentation network, a

existing methods on the HKS dataset, while also providing a comprehensive

Our proposed model combines a unique attention mechanism with a novel feature called 'temporal instance attention', allowing it to focus on specific instances in the video where accidents are more likely to occur. By applying temporal instance attention in conjunction with a region-based approach, the model can accurately identify high-risk areas within each frame. Finally, the fusion of spatial and temporal features enables the system to make more accurate predictions. When tested on the CrashRiskNet dataset, our proposed system achieved outstanding results, demonstrating a 96.44% accuracy rate, which is a significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art model. Recent advances in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have made it possible to create realistic synthetic images, which are expected to significantly impact the field of computer vision. However, generating high-quality images using GANs often proves to be challenging, as unsupervised approaches often fail to produce realistic results, while supervised methods can produce images that don't match their input supervision. This paper presents a novel approach to improve the quality of synthetic images by learning from both the distribution of input images and the labels associated with them. Our results show that this approach produces images that are semantically consistent with their input and exhibit improved quality compared to other GAN methods. Our approach is particularly useful in situations where labels are available, which can facilitate the creation of synthetic images with specific attributes. Recent research has highlighted the vulnerability of large language models to minor structural changes or random distortions, which can significantly degrade their performance. In this work, we explore the benefits of multitask learning (MTL) in enhancing the robustness of language models to random neuron failures. Our experiments demonstrate that training language models on multiple tasks simultaneously not only improves their performance on individual tasks but also makes them more resilient to such neuron failures, allowing them to maintain most of their performance loss. Moreover, MTL enables the model to identify task-specific neurons that are critical for each specific task, which can then be protected from damage. Our findings indicate that this increased robustness to neuron failures in language models is a natural byproduct of the task-interplay facilitated by MTL, and we identify key factors that contribute to this effect. Our research has the potential to inspire new techniques for improving the robustness of language models to random neuron failures. The proliferation of Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices has raised significant privacy concerns among individuals, prompting a pressing need for effective privacy preservation mechanisms. Given the diverse nature of IoT applications, a versatile privacy preservation framework is essential to ensure secure and private data processing. To address this critical challenge, we introduce a novel framework for preserving privacy in IoT services, enabling seamless and secure data sharing between IoT devices and services while guaranteeing confidentiality. Our proposed framework is based on a novel protocol, enabling devices to obtain information without revealing sensitive user data, and a corresponding service to conceal and transmit user information with enhanced security. Our protocol, grounded in the concept of zero-knowledge proof, provides a secure basis for developing diverse privacy-preserving services, ensuring the integrity and confidentiality of user data. Our framework is further enhanced by a privacy-aware service discovery mechanism, enabling users to identify suitable services that align with their privacy requirements. A comprehensive evaluation of our framework demonstrates its effectiveness in safeguarding user privacy. Our research contributes to the development of a comprehensive and secure framework for privacy preservation in the IoT ecosystem. Visual Question Answering is a complex task that demands the integration of cutting-edge techniques from computer vision and natural language processing to deliver accurate results. Despite their effectiveness in individual applications, these approaches often fall short when applied in conjunction with others. In this research, we introduce a novel framework, VQA-Graph, which effectively combines multiple methodologies to achieve state-of-the-art performance. By extracting key information from visual inputs and transforming them into graph structures, we represent these graphs as graphs of concepts. We then utilize a transformer-based model to analyze these concepts and generate answers, achieving top scores in two benchmark VQA challenges. Results reveal that our approach surpasses the performance of the current state of the art across multiple evaluation metrics. Additionally, our model demonstrates robustness in handling diverse visual and semantic scenarios. Notably, we achieve a record score of 64.7% accuracy on the OK-VQA challenge, which is the most challenging VQA benchmark to date. which are the foundation for both logical and physical data storage systems.
