and those that reorder data (sorting). Building on this classification, we have 
developed a unified framework for designing efficient algorithms to perform 
these operations, which involves considering the maximum size of intermediate 
results. This approach enables us to select the most suitable algorithm for 
each operation based on the size of the input data. Additionally, we have 
developed a method for combining multiple operations into a single optimized 
query, which involves considering both intermediate result size and input 
data size. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective in reducing query 
execution times for both small and large inputs. The study also highlights 
the potential for further optimization by considering both size constraints 
and the amount of data being processed. Our findings are supported by an 
extensive analysis of 11,000 queries from a real-world database server log. 
The results show that our optimized queries can be up to 2.5 times faster 
than existing implementations for small inputs and up to 1.4 times faster 
for larger inputs. Furthermore, we have developed a tool that can automatically 
apply these optimizations to real-world queries, which can be accessed through 
our public repository. This tool can also be integrated into existing database 
systems to enhance their performance. Our research has the potential to 
significantly improve the performance of relational operations in database 
systems. We have also developed a method for integrating our optimization 
approach into existing database servers, which can be used to improve the 
performance of database queries. Our approach is expected to be widely 
adoptable and beneficial to both researchers and developers working on data 
management systems. Our work has the potential to support further research 
on optimizing database queries and improving the performance of data storage 
systems. Our approach is not limited to the specific operations we have focused 
on, but rather provides a general framework for optimizing database queries. 
We believe that our work will contribute significantly to the advancement of 
relational databases and query optimization. Our research has the potential 
to improve the performance of database queries and make them more efficient.

This study introduces an innovative approach to emotion recognition from speech
utilizing a transfer learning method with a deep neural network initially trained
through image processing. The proposed architecture incorporates two distinct layers
of visual processing - one focused on acoustic frequencies and the other on audio
duration - in addition to a fully connected, hierarchical classification module.
The model's parameters are trained using the AudioMD dataset, and its effectiveness
is assessed across three languages - English, Mandarin, and French - utilizing respective emotional speech corpora.
The proposed method yields superior results compared to a conventional DNN model,
achieving average accuracy improvements of 3.7% on the IEMOCAP dataset in English,
2.9% on the IIIT-JMR database in Mandarin, and 5.5% on the Multimodal EmotionDB
database in French, using only 20% of the training data. The model's ability to
transfer effectively across languages and acoustic characteristics further highlights
the potential of this transfer learning method in enhancing emotional speech
recognition using deep neural networks. The proposed architecture's source code and
trained models are openly available for further research at https://github.com/sofgeorgiev/transfer_acoustic_dnn.

illumination conditions. The proposed method is based on a multi-stage framework

This paper presents a multi-task sequence prediction system that simultaneously predicts four levels of annotation: punctuation marks and two types of linguistic features associated with Tunisian Arabizi characters. The annotation levels are then combined to form a normalized and standardized text. We propose a unified approach that unifies the prediction tasks for all annotation types, allowing for a single training process. The system utilizes a neural network architecture that incorporates recurrent units to process input sequences at different levels. The system's performance is evaluated using a gold-standard dataset annotated with various linguistic features by multiple native speakers. The results show that the system achieves high accuracy in predicting each type of annotation feature separately and in normalizing Arabizi text when using a training dataset that includes all annotation levels. The system's performance is further enhanced by using a supervised pre-training method on a related task, resulting in improved results when using a smaller Arabizi dataset compared to English. Finally, we demonstrate the system's applicability by using it to predict punctuation marks on a test dataset and presenting the system's performance metrics. The system's source code is publicly available on GitHub. https://github.com/sghazza/ArabiziNormalization. The performance of algebraic multigrid (AMG) methods heavily relies on the accuracy and choice of various parameters, particularly the interpolation operator. In this study, we present a linear machine learning approach to generate an AMG interpolation operator on unstructured, triangular meshes. Our proposed operator is a linear combination of basic interpolation operators, and its coefficients are obtained through linear machine learning regression, using a dataset of small to moderate-sized problems solved by an arbitrary multigrid method. Our experiments demonstrate that this technique can significantly improve the AMG method's performance without requiring the target problem, showcasing its ability to adapt to diverse input data. Furthermore, our method allows for the application of learned interpolation operators to various AMG solvers operating on different element types. Our results show substantial speedup and accuracy improvements compared to standard AMG approaches. Additionally, this technique can be combined with other machine learning strategies to generate a more comprehensive and robust AMG solver. The presented method is also transferable to other types of partial differential equations and can be applied to various other solvers operating on these problems. The introduction of Large-scale Deterministic IP Networks, enabled by the SRv6 protocol, has brought large-scale data center networking one step closer to fulfilling its promise of deterministic assurance, relying heavily on the SRv6 Segment ID for its functioning. However, the SRv6 protocol's complex architecture and large address pool necessitate the development of user-friendly tools to facilitate the process of configuring and verifying the network paths. In response to this need, we present a new tool called GraphDB that offers an intuitive representation of SRv6 graphs, allowing users to create and modify paths through the creation of Binding Tables and Forwarding Graph Yards. Moreover, GraphDB's ability to compute and display the Forwarding Table further streamlines the process of configuring network routes. By enabling users to define multiple Binding Tables and associated Forwarding Graph Yards, GraphDB also enables the creation and verification of diverse network paths. We have successfully demonstrated the efficacy of GraphDB through a series of experiments, showcasing its capabilities in managing and verifying SRv6 graphs. Furthermore, the tool's potential to be integrated with existing network protocols, such as MPLS, has also been highlighted, providing a more efficient and user-friendly alternative to traditional network configurations. In conclusion, the development of GraphDB has marked a significant step forward in the field of network configuration and verification, offering a more intuitive and efficient solution for managing complex network configurations. The tool's source code is available for download at a public repository. https://github.com/ashishp1111/srv6_graphdb. Advanced reinforcement learning systems, like those using deep learning models, are able to navigate complex problems but raise concerns about their ability to achieve optimal outcomes in situations where goals are unclear or changing. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for dynamic state estimation in power networks, which leverages low-rank tensor decomposition to efficiently and accurately estimate both system states and network topology. The proposed method accounts for the interplay between state estimation and graph topology estimation, resulting in accelerated convergence and improved robustness against measurement errors. A decoupled approach, which updates network topology and states separately, can become stuck in local optima and requires careful initialization, whereas the coupled framework provides a unified solution that necessitates no special starting point initialization, achieving a significant 3x reduction in iteration count while producing more accurate results than the decoupled method. Moreover, the coupled framework exhibits superior robustness to errors in network topology estimation, outperforming the decoupled method in various scenarios. Specifically, when dealing with small measurement errors, the coupled framework achieves a significant 10x improvement in accuracy. The proposed method has been extensively validated using the IEEE 14-bus test network, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling both synchrophasor and non-synchrophasor measurements. Our research demonstrates that a severe currency drop in a worker's country leads to positive real returns for that worker in the platform, thus reversing the well-known terms of the Gains from Trade. We suggest that this unexpected outcome occurs because many platforms, including online labor marketplaces, span cross-border and intra-firm boundaries. The ongoing growth in the number of processing cores has led to increased demand for efficient parallelization techniques.  However, existing approaches often fall short, struggling to effectively handle large numbers of tasks, mitigate scheduling errors, and overcome memory limitations.  To address these challenges, we developed a new parallelization framework that utilizes multiresolution modeling.  Specifically, we have implemented and evaluated an innovative technique that utilizes self-similar patterns in multiresolution graphs to optimize the execution of multithreaded programs.  Through our experiments, we have demonstrated that this approach can effectively reduce thread synchronization overheads and improve code performance, resulting in a 1.2 to 3.9 fold improvement in code execution speed.  Notably, our technique has been successfully applied to real-world programs, including those written in Fortran, C, and Java.  Furthermore, we have made the parallelization framework and experimental results publicly available. We introduce an original neural network architecture for processing
three-dimensional atomic structures. To preserve the structure's key properties,
our design ensures that the neural network's parameters remain unchanged under
translations and rotations in three-dimensional space. This translational and
rotational equivariance is achieved by incorporating a differentiable layer
that maps points and directions to a high-dimensional space, allowing us to
propose an element-wise equivariant layer that maintains the response's vector
properties under rotations. We demonstrate that our proposed neural network
achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting a material's mechanical
properties from its three-dimensional atomic configuration. We also show that
the neural network's internal representations exhibit the desired equivariance
properties and can be used to identify the material's relevant degrees of
freedom. This research marks the first application of equivariant neural
networks to study mechanical properties of materials with an interpretability
focus. We believe that the developed methods will be instrumental in creating
more accurate and interpretable machine learning models for studying
interactions between materials and their environment. The code and data used in
this research are publicly available at https://github.com/andreasobel/equivariant-ml.

A common approach to reducing model size involves transferring knowledge from a complex model to a simpler one, and numerous studies have explored this method. However, the underlying mechanisms behind knowledge distillation are not yet fully understood. In this study, we investigate the connection between the effectiveness of knowledge distillation and the mutual information between the input, model representation, and target output. We also propose a novel distillation method that can be used to reduce both model size and computational costs. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach can create lightweight models with equivalent capabilities to larger models. For example, the model we trained on the CIFAR-10 dataset using our method achieved 97.77% top-1 accuracy, comparable to a model with 2.46M parameters that reached 97.53%. In contrast, the traditional knowledge distillation method using ResNet-50 achieved 93.80% accuracy, indicating a 3.53% improvement. We also found that the mutual information between the input and model representation increased from 0.69 bits to 1.46 bits, and that from the model to the target output increased from 0.27 bits to 0.58 bits. These results confirm that our method can effectively reduce model size while maintaining performance. In addition, we discovered that the mutual information between the input and model representation is a reliable indicator of model capacity, and that it can be used to predict model performance in real-time. We also found that the mutual information between the model and target output can be used to predict model accuracy. Our findings provide new insights into the effectiveness of knowledge distillation and the connection between mutual information and model performance. We believe that our work will contribute to a deeper understanding of knowledge distillation and its applications in model compression. In particular, we hope that our method of reducing mutual information will inspire further research into model compression and pruning. Automated analysis of electron microscopy datasets is an arduous task, particularly in cases involving massive datasets.  A potential solution to this problem lies in the application of machine learning techniques, which can automate the process of image processing and interpretation.  This study focuses on the automated analysis of whole-mount EM images of cells utilizing a technique called connective tracking.  Initially, we employed a pre-trained neural network to generate an enhanced version of the raw EM image.  Subsequently, we used this processed image to train a second neural network, which would output the precise boundaries of various cellular components.  Through our experiments, we achieved a mean intersection-over-union score of 0.65 for cell boundaries and 0.80 for nuclear boundaries.  Furthermore, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach by successfully segmenting cellular components in whole-mount EM images from diverse cell types, including human embryonic stem cells and the immunoglobulin-producing B cell line 38D22.  Our findings suggest that deep learning holds great promise in the automated analysis of whole-mount EM images.  As a result, we anticipate that machine learning techniques will revolutionize the field of EM image analysis, enabling researchers to process massive datasets with unprecedented speed and efficiency.  This, in turn, will facilitate the discovery of novel cellular structures and shed new light on cellular organization.  Our research represents a significant step towards achieving this goal. We introduce a novel method for efficiently optimizing the accuracy and power consumption of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) on Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs). Our approach, known as PARETO, is the first to simultaneously optimize the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency in DNNs. PARETO is a highly scalable framework that can seamlessly integrate with various FPGA accelerators, even those with limited resources. By utilizing Pareto-front optimization techniques, PARETO dynamically balances accuracy with energy consumption. We evaluate PARETO on the AlexNet and VGG16 models and observe significant improvements in accuracy, energy consumption, and inference speed, across multiple FPGA accelerators. On the Xilinx Versal UE100, PARETO outperforms state-of-the-art solutions by up to 1.5 times in accuracy, 2.6 times in energy consumption, and 1.7 times in inference speed. A comprehensive study of the effects of FPGA architecture, DNN model, and Pareto-front optimization techniques is also presented. The findings show that self-supervised learning can yield comparable or superior performance to supervised learning, especially when minority classes are adequately represented. Furthermore, the research reveals that self-supervised learning can produce more robust models capable of generalizing to minority classes, even when using fewer data samples. In this study, we develop a policy learning algorithm called the minimum action diffusion (MAD) framework, which is suitable for non-stationary environments with continuous action spaces. MAD builds on the idea of using the diffusion map to approximate the stationary value function, and then uses this approximation to find the optimal policy. We prove that MAD converges in on-policy settings and outperforms traditional reinforcement learning methods, such as soft actor-critic (SAC), in offline policy evaluation. We also show that MAD is effective in adapting to changing environments through simulation results on continuous control tasks. In addition, we propose a practical MAD algorithm called MAD-BC, which combines model-based and model-free approaches for improved performance. The results of this study demonstrate the effectiveness of the MAD framework, which offers a new perspective on value-based reinforcement learning. This study explores how various distributed systems can securely perform the task of averaging inputs using linearly separable functions, while in a distributed environment. We analyze two scenarios: one in which the function used for aggregation remains unchanged but multiple agents contribute unique inputs, and the other scenario where both inputs and aggregation functions change from one round to the next. We demonstrate that adding randomness to previous work on linearly separable functions is necessary to prevent malicious agents from controlling the aggregation result in the first scenario, and we show how existing results can still be applied in the second scenario by using previous work as an input to a simple hash function. Additionally, we investigate the potential to leverage past results as inputs, which could further enhance the security of these systems. We also consider the practicality of these enhanced methods, which we verified by conducting experiments on various hardware platforms. Ultimately, we conclude that adding randomness to existing results is a simple yet effective way to improve the security of these systems, which can be implemented with minimal additional resources. Our research findings are complemented by a publicly available software implementation on GitHub. We also discuss potential future research directions that could further strengthen the security of these distributed systems. The associated codebase can be found at https://github.com/ashish-geek/secure_avg.

Our results suggest that our deep learning approach has the potential to significantly improve the diagnosis and prognosis of brain gliomas. Our approach relies on the observation that some data is inherently linked to external variables, such as transportation schedules, while other information remains independent. By using linear regression to analyze and eliminate non-reliable data, we demonstrate that our method can effectively improve the accuracy of transportation scheduling systems. Our results indicate a substantial improvement in scheduling reliability, including a 30% reduction in scheduling errors and a 20% increase in reliable schedules. Ultimately, this technique can be applied to numerous other systems where incomplete data is a major issue. This is made possible by aligning the clothing by its geometric features, such as seams and patterns, rather than general structures, resulting in more accurate and versatile results. This framework's potential is showcased through various examples, including aligning and transforming different clothing, as well as generating new styles.
